summary: The two men never met. Dostoevsky discussed Anna Karenina at length in A Writer's Diary (1877), and Tolstoy, in a letter to Strakhov, named The House of the Dead the summit of modern prose. Since Merezhkovsky (1901–02), a comparative tradition has read the two as opposite poles of the Western novel — life observed from outside and a voice pouring out from within — a tradition that runs on through George Steiner.

Chekhov visited Tolstoy at Yasnaya Polyana in 1895 and met him often in the Crimea in 1901–02 as well. Tolstoy regarded his short stories as the summit of Russian prose, but could never stand his plays. Chekhov himself wrote in his letters that he had been deeply moved by Tolstoy's moral philosophy and then worked his way free of it after his journey to Sakhalin.

Modern drama's two starting points were built in opposite directions. Ibsen tightened his plays with retrospective plots in which a hidden past collapses the present, while Chekhov removed the resolution of events altogether and left only conversation that talks past itself. Theater history writing since Raymond Williams places the two side by side as the two branches into which twentieth-century dramaturgy split.

James lived in Paris in 1875–76 and attended Flaubert's Sunday gatherings, meeting him in person, and in the essay 'Gustave Flaubert' in Notes on Novelists (1914) he defined him as 'the novelist's novelist.' Flaubert's discipline of pushing the author's commentary outside the sentence is a direct forerunner of what James formulated, in the prefaces to the New York Edition, as point-of-view control and dramatization.

James wrote several essays on Ibsen, including 'On the Occasion of Hedda Gabler' in The New Review in 1891, and around the same time took up playwriting himself. Ibsen's method of interrogating society's lies through drawing-room dialogue alone carried over into the scene-centered construction that James, in his late novels, called 'dramatization.'

The two men lived as neighbors in Kent and Sussex and visited each other. Conrad wrote 'Henry James: An Appreciation' in 1905, setting him up as a master of prose, and James, in 'The New Novel' in 1914, examined the layered narrator structure of Chance point by point. This exchange of reading and public commentary pushed forward the English novel's experiments with point of view.

It is the standard account in Conrad studies that Conrad carried the sentence discipline of the French novel — exact words and a suppressed narrator — over into English prose. The goal set out in his 1897 novel preface, 'above all, to make you see,' is likewise read within the observational discipline of the Flaubert–Maupassant line. Conrad's own statements naming Flaubert as a master are fragmentary even within his letters, however, so this is recorded only at the level of scholarly consensus.

Conrad openly disliked Dostoevsky, writing to Edward Garnett that he found him unbearable, but Under Western Eyes is read as a novel that writes back against Crime and Punishment, built on the axes of confession and betrayal. Treating this design, which rejects both Russian autocracy and the revolutionaries at once, as a confrontation with Dostoevsky is the standard point in Conrad studies.

In 1857 the two men stood trial for indecency within months of each other. That October, Baudelaire published a review of Madame Bovary in L'Artiste, discussing what the novel had built in the place where sentiment had been removed, and Flaubert, on receiving The Flowers of Evil, wrote back that it had made Romanticism young again. This exchange over each other's books survives.

In early 1887, Nietzsche happened to pick up a French edition of Notes from Underground in a bookshop in Nice, and in a letter to Overbeck on February 23 he described the discovery as a great stroke of luck in his life. In Twilight of the Idols, he calls Dostoevsky the only psychologist he ever learned anything from. Dostoevsky's character type — excessive self-consciousness that betrays its own interest — enters directly into the psychological vocabulary of Nietzsche's late work.

In his 1888 notebooks, Nietzsche copied out passages of Baudelaire's prose and names him as the first person in France to champion Wagner. That the vocabulary of Nietzsche's late years, which treats decadence not as pathology but as a form proper to the age, took shape by way of Baudelaire is a point that Nietzsche philology argues from the notebooks.

American poetry's two starting points were built without either knowing the other. In an 1862 letter to Higginson, Dickinson wrote that she had never read Whitman's book and had heard that he was indecent. A long line that swallows the whole nation through catalogued repetition, against ten lines broken by the dash within hymn meter — this split into opposite directions in the same country at the same time is a basic axis of American poetry history.

In a letter to Felice in September 1913, Kafka named Dostoevsky as one of his four 'true blood relatives.' The structure of guilt in Crime and Punishment, narrating the consciousness of the interrogated from within, resonates deeply with the premise of The Trial.

Flaubert is also among the same four 'true blood relatives' named in that 1913 letter. Kafka read Flaubert in French and was especially fond of Sentimental Education, and he took as the standard for his own prose sentences that record only the facts precisely, without commenting on the feeling.

At eighteen, Joyce published 'Ibsen's New Drama' (The Fortnightly Review, April 1900), discussing When We Dead Awaken, and when Ibsen sent his thanks through his translator William Archer, Joyce wrote back the following March, on Ibsen's birthday, in Norwegian — a language he had learned in order to read him in the original. What he took from Ibsen was a sense of what a prose-realist play could interrogate.

The passage near the end of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man that likens the artist to a god who withdraws behind creation to pare his fingernails carries over, almost verbatim, Flaubert's 1852 letter to Louise Colet stating that the artist must be everywhere in the work and visible nowhere, like God in creation. Joyce scholarship treats this lineage together as the route by which free indirect discourse was passed down.

When the twenty-year-old Joyce met the thirty-seven-year-old Yeats in Dublin in 1902, the encounter survives as the anecdote of Joyce bluntly declaring his elder too old, but Yeats went on to connect him with Arthur Symons and Pound and arranged literary-fund support for him. In 1932 Yeats invited him to join the Irish Academy of Letters, and Joyce declined.

In January 1920, Proust published 'On Flaubert's "Style"' in the NRF, reading Flaubert as a writer who inscribed the very passage of time into grammar through nothing more than the alternation of imperfect and simple past tenses and a sparing use of conjunctions. This essay, which defends Flaubert by reducing him to a question of style, is also the most direct document in which Proust explained the principles of his own sentences.

The Captive contains a passage in which the narrator explains at length to Albertine what is new in Dostoevsky. In this episode, Proust discusses, by comparison with painting, the method of presenting a character not through explanation but through the house he lives in and the composition of a scene, and the tradition of Proust commentary treats this episode as the standard basis for linking the two writers.

In 'The Russian Point of View,' in The Common Reader (1925), Woolf explained why Chekhov's stories seem to end without a resolution as a matter of shifting emphasis. This method of making a shift in perception, rather than an event, the unit of narrative is the same principle that organizes her own short stories and Mrs Dalloway.

Together with S. S. Koteliansky, Woolf translated the suppressed chapter from Demons and published it as Stavrogin's Confession (1922) through the Hogarth Press. This co-translation, carried out while she was learning Russian, shows directly the route by which British modernism absorbed the Russian novel.

In 1922, Woolf wrote to Roger Fry that Proust stirred her own desire for expression so much that she could hardly write a sentence. The year she spent reading In Search of Lost Time overlaps with the period she was conceiving Mrs Dalloway, and afterward her prose takes on a way of carrying the fine tremor of perception through the length of a sentence.

Born in the same year, 1882, the two writers each published, within three years of each other, a novel that covers a single day. Woolf wrote in her diary that Ulysses was the work of an uneducated man, but on the problem of carrying consciousness into sentences, the two solved the same task with opposite temperaments — encyclopedic accumulation and a shifting style chapter by chapter, versus a restrained free indirect discourse. Modernism scholarship always treats this contrast together.

The Hogarth Press published Mansfield's 'Prelude' in 1918 as one of its early publications, and the two women were friends and rivals who read each other's work with a jealous eye. After Mansfield's death, Woolf wrote in her diary that it was the only writing she had ever been jealous of.

Throughout her diaries and letters, Mansfield took Chekhov as the standard for her own short stories, and she established in the English-speaking world his structure of ending on a shift in perception rather than a twist of plot. How close her early story 'The Child-Who-Was-Tired' (1910) comes to Chekhov's 'Sleepy' remains a matter of debate even now.

In his 1947 lecture 'Nietzsche's Philosophy in the Light of Our Experience,' Mann treated Nietzsche simultaneously as the intellectual premise of his own generation and as an accomplice in the German catastrophe. To Leverkühn, the composer of Doctor Faustus, Nietzsche's biography — infection with syphilis and the collapse of his mind — is assigned almost without alteration.

In his 1921 Lübeck lecture 'Goethe and Tolstoy,' Mann grouped the two together as epic writers who emerged from nature, and placed the lineage he belonged to on the opposite side. In effect he used Tolstoy as a coordinate to fix the position of his own fiction, and the dialogic construction of The Magic Mountain was likewise designed on this contrast.

In 'Dostoevsky — in Moderation,' his introduction to an English-language Dostoevsky anthology, Mann read him, alongside Nietzsche, as a writer who arrived at insight through illness. This reading underlies his construction of Doctor Faustus as a bargain that trades artistic mastery for disease.

In a 1956 Paris Review interview, Faulkner named Conrad as a writer he reread every year. A framed structure in which the narrator relays events without fully understanding them, and a decoding that only resolves belatedly, are carried directly into the narrative design of Absalom, Absalom!

In the 1957–58 question-and-answer sessions at the University of Virginia, Faulkner said Ulysses should be read with the same faith one reads the Bible, and testimony survives that he had already read it in the early 1920s. Interior monologue without quotation marks and a style that shifts with each narrator carried over into the four-part construction of The Sound and the Fury.

In his diaries, Musil recorded the shock of reading Nietzsche's collected works in his youth. The method of describing morality not as a given fact but as something historically made carries over, in The Man Without Qualities, into an essayism that suspends judgment and develops thought alone.

Scholarship on the European modernist novel treats In Search of Lost Time and The Man Without Qualities together. This is because they share the same condition: perception and thought fill the narrative in place of the progress of events, and each is a vast novel whose completion was left suspended by its author's death. There is no record of direct contact between the two men.

Pessoa wrote 'Salutation to Walt Whitman' under the name of his heteronym Álvaro de Campos, and the runaway catalogues and exclamations of 'Maritime Ode' are Whitman's long line carried over into Portuguese. The persona of Campos itself is designed to carry a Whitmanesque expansiveness.

In 1902, Yeats read the Nietzsche that John Quinn had sent him and wrote to Lady Gregory that he was a powerful magician completing Blake. The scheme of the opposing self, or mask, that he took from this leads on into the symbolic system of A Vision and into the hard tone of his late poetry, which discarded aesthetic haziness.

Rilke traveled to Russia twice, in 1899 and 1900, visiting Tolstoy on both occasions, and left an account of his visit to Yasnaya Polyana in his letters. The Russian experience he gained on these journeys — the form of prayer and a pilgrim speaker — shaped the idiom of The Book of Hours.

In The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge, Malte invokes Baudelaire's 'A Carcass' to write that the poet must not look away even before something horrifying, but must see the being within it. Given that Rilke calls up the same poem again in his 1907 letters on Cézanne, the discipline of the thing-poem came not only from Rodin and Cézanne but from Baudelaire as well.

In 'Baudelaire,' his 1930 introduction to Christopher Isherwood's translation of Intimate Journals, Eliot defined him as the first poet to make the ugliness of the city the material of poetry and as a poet who restored the reality of good and evil. The line 'hypocrite reader' at the end of Part I of The Waste Land is lifted directly from the prefatory poem of The Flowers of Evil.

In the first Yeats lecture, delivered at the Abbey Theatre in 1940, Eliot cited Yeats, who overhauled his style entirely in old age, as the most important example his generation possessed. The passage on the familiar compound ghost in 'Little Gidding,' from Four Quartets, is read as the place where he calls that Yeats back to stand before him.

The epigraph of The Waste Land was originally the final cry from Heart of Darkness, and it was dropped at Pound's objection that Conrad did not carry enough weight. Traces of this survive in the facsimile of the drafts. Three years later, the line announcing Kurtz's death resurfaces as the epigraph of 'The Hollow Men.'

In 'Ulysses, Order, and Myth,' published in The Dial in November 1923, Eliot named the method of using myth as a frame that gives shape to contemporary chaos the 'mythical method,' and proposed it as a substitute for narrative form. It is the essay in which he used Joyce to explain the principle by which The Waste Land was assembled.

In her 1934–35 lecture tour of America, Stein singled out Henry James as the pioneer who first found the literary method of the twentieth century, and traced her own lineage back to him. In making the sentence carry the progress of cognition rather than event, the two writers held onto the same problem.

Stein wrote in The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas that around the time she began writing Three Lives, she was translating Flaubert's 'A Simple Heart' as a translation exercise. The design of that story, which records a servant woman's life without emotional commentary, carried over into the construction of her own first book, which places three women's lives side by side.

Ibsen erected an invisible fourth wall facing the audience and interrogated the drawing room from within it, while Pirandello sent unfinished characters bursting onto the stage and tore that wall down from the inside. Modern drama scholarship describes Pirandello's metatheater as an inversion of the realist stage Ibsen had established. Pirandello himself ranked Ibsen as a playwright second only to Shakespeare, so this contrast is a matter of opposing forms, not personal enmity.

There is no record of direct contact between the novelist from Rio de Janeiro and the playwright from Sicily. This atlas places the two near each other because they share the same method of treating the self as the sum of roles assigned by other people — Dom Casmurro hands the verdict on whether the wife betrayed him off to the reader, while One, No One and One Hundred Thousand begins again from the place where the name is lost.

Brecht's epic theater took aim at the entire dramaturgy that draws the audience into the stage's illusion, and its standard form was Ibsen's drawing-room drama. This is also why Raymond Williams drew the trajectory of modern drama running from Ibsen to Brecht.

Scholarship on twentieth-century anti-illusionist theater treats the two together. Pirandello exposed the stage's apparatus of representation through the play within the play, while Brecht broke immersion with songs and titles. Their purposes diverged — one sought to show the indeterminacy of identity, the other the mutability of history. No direct contact between the two men has been confirmed.

The Jerusalem chapters of The Master and Margarita interrogate how power processes truth, taking up the problem set established by the Grand Inquisitor episode in The Brothers Karamazov. Reading this design, which seats the devil in the judge's place, within the Dostoevsky lineage is the standard point in Bulgakov studies.

Lorca included 'Ode to Walt Whitman' in Poet in New York, written during his 1929–30 stay in New York. To sing of the labor and bodies that the city of capital had trampled, he borrowed Whitman's long line and mode of address directly, while at the same time setting that voice against the hypocrisy of his own era.
